Verify rewrite DATA ONLY. Do not write improved examples or solve the user's task.
Read every input and target in full. Return one review per exact id and row_sha256.
input_verdict checks plausible natural drafts or dictation, recoverable intent, contradictions,
fake noise, padding and leaked authoring instructions. output_verdict checks natural appropriate
language and formatting. pair_verdict checks ALL facts, uncertainty, conditions, negation,
quantities, names, quotations, literals, requests versus assertions, and the supplied mode.
/transcribe permits punctuation, true disfluency removal and explicit corrections, not lexical
paraphrasing. Preserve meaningful words like German 'um' and 'er', colloquial Portuguese and
unfinished thoughts. /slack is casual minimal cleanup; a long input may be a pasted thread.
/prompt reorganizes a self-contained request and never answers it. It must not drop supplied
material, hedges or constraints. /polish improves prose without omissions or changed certainty.
Identity inputs must remain byte-identical. Apply only supplied dictionary/profile context.
Check long texts paragraph by paragraph. Fail concrete defects. Uncertain means not confidently
justifiable. Pass requires no material defect. Overall verdict is fail if any dimension fails,
uncertain if any dimension is uncertain and none fails, otherwise pass. Give a concrete critique
for EVERY pair, citing the changed detail for defects. These are model judgments, not human labels.

new paragraph before we closed the folder i read the condition back to jonah and mara if a date is still unconfirmed at wednesday noon the badge stays at the desk and does not go in the outgoing envelope jonah said quote yes especially for the annex because they cannot send the badge back before the next delivery end quote mara wrote the time in the margin beside the pending entries and put the meeting pad in the front pocket the blue clipboard stayed by the sink for the morning users and the folder went back into the locked cabinet nobody changed the four pages during the meeting the remaining work is to check the new date answers, compare the safety register, and forward the shared studio access list while keeping the unconfirmed badges at the desk", "output": "So this is the account of forwarding the shared studio access list for the west rooms before the winter open house and the repair workshops that follow it. The list belongs to the people who use the building, not to one department, and that point came up again at the meeting on Tuesday at six in the small print room. The current copy was on a blue clipboard beside the sink and had thirty-eight names across four pages. Mara Ellis had checked the spelling against the paper cards at the front desk, but she had not checked which dates each person could come in. The studio manager, Jonah Reed, asked me to forward the list to the door team by Thursday morning so they could prepare the temporary badges. He said, “Please send the working copy first and keep the old sheet in the folder until the door team confirms they can read it.” I said I would forward the copy after checking the date column and the notes about guests.

The access list covers the print room, the wood room, the washout bay, and the shared loading corridor. People can use more than one room, but a badge does not open every room by default. The print room is open to all listed members during staffed hours. The wood room needs a separate safety mark beside a person's name, and the washout bay stays locked when the ventilation service is running. Those details were on the second page in a box written by Priya Sen, who coordinates equipment training. Mara said the old blue clipboard had no box and that two people had mistaken a general building badge for permission to enter the wood room. I checked the three names she pointed out and found that only one had the safety mark. The other two had booked an introduction but had not completed it. Jonah asked us to keep the names on the list while the training dates remained unconfirmed.

The date column matters because the door team prints badges for specific shifts rather than for the whole season. If a person can come only on Saturday, that should appear beside the person's name and not in the comments field. On the last page, several entries said “evenings” but did not say which day. Mara had collected those notes during the summer, and she did not know whether each person still wanted an evening slot. She said, “I can ask the three people who left a phone number, but I do not want to guess for everyone else.” Jonah said we could forward the list with those entries marked pending and add a short note to the door team. The condition we agreed on was that if anyone had not confirmed a date by Wednesday at noon, the badge should be held at the desk and should not be put in the outgoing envelope. This condition was important because the envelope goes to the annex once each afternoon.

At the meeting, I checked the page numbers against the sign-in book and found a gap between page two and page three. The missing page was not a list of people; it was the equipment key showing which rooms required a staff escort. Priya had taken the key page home to compare its safety marks with the training register and planned to bring it back on Wednesday morning. She had told Jonah that the register included two recent wood room orientations that were not yet copied onto the blue clipboard. Jonah said not to add those marks based on a message alone and asked Priya to bring the register so the entries could be checked together. Mara wrote that note on the meeting pad. I left the names unchanged and added a pencil mark beside the two entries that needed review so nobody would mistake them for completed training.

I then looked at the guest notes because the open house brings visitors who are not regular studio members. The current wording says guests must stay with the person who signed them in and may not use powered equipment. That wording came from the building safety sheet, and Jonah did not ask us to change it. A member can list one guest for the open house, but the member has to be present at arrival. The door team wanted a separate count of those guests so they could set aside paper visitor badges. Mara found four guest names on the last page and one entry that said “plus family” without a number. She said, “I know the person who wrote that, but I do not know how many people they mean.” We left that entry as written and marked it for a question rather than counting it as one guest or several.

The folder for the working copy is in the locked cabinet under the reception counter, and it has a green tab marked “winter access.” The older sheets are in a separate envelope with the month written on the front. Jonah said the old sheets should stay there because a few former members still come by to collect personal tools, and the desk needs a record of the dates when their badges were returned. Mara counted the returned badge cards in the envelope and found eleven cards with initials but no return date. She put a note in the folder asking the desk staff to check the return log before moving any of those cards. The log is kept beside the daily key sheet, and the desk staff update it after closing on weekdays. The Saturday volunteer makes a note on paper and gives it to Jonah on Monday.

The door team needs a readable scan as well as the paper working copy because the annex printer has been unreliable this week. I checked that each page sat flat and that the blue clipboard did not cover the initials at the bottom of page four. The scanner in the print room saves files to the shared drive under Building, then Access, then Winter Open House. Priya said the scanner sometimes crops the right edge if the paper is fed with the punched side first, so I used the glass and checked the preview before saving it. The file name on the drive was “winter access west rooms draft two,” and Jonah asked me to keep that name when I forwarded it. He did not want a new final label because the dates and two safety marks still needed checking.

We wrote down the handoff steps before leaving the print room:
1. Mara will ask the three people with incomplete date notes whether they can confirm a weekday or Saturday slot.
2. Priya will bring the safety register and the equipment key page on Wednesday morning.
3. I will check the corrected date entries against the answers Mara receives and will forward the list to the door team by Thursday morning.
4. Jonah will collect the door team's questions and keep them with the working copy.

The list itself will not be replaced with a clean version until the date answers and safety marks have been checked together. Those steps let the door team begin preparing the pages without treating a pencilled note as a confirmed entry.

Before we closed the folder, I read the condition back to Jonah and Mara: if a date is still unconfirmed at Wednesday noon, the badge stays at the desk and does not go in the outgoing envelope. Jonah said, “Yes, especially for the annex because they cannot send the badge back before the next delivery.” Mara wrote the time in the margin beside the pending entries and put the meeting pad in the front pocket. The blue clipboard stayed by the sink for the morning users, and the folder went back into the locked cabinet. Nobody changed the four pages during the meeting. The remaining work is to check the new date answers, compare the safety register, and forward the shared studio access list while keeping the unconfirmed badges at the desk."}]
